questions.question: Write down the mathematical model of the set covering problem. Describe the physical meaning of the constraint sets in the mathematical model. [3 + 1 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Set $S = \{1, \dots, n\}$ of items and subsets $S_1, \dots, S_m$ of $S$; choosing $S_j$ costs $c_j > 0$; pick subsets that cover every item at minimum cost.
Data: $a_{ij} = 1$ if item $i$ is in $S_j$, $a_{ij} = 0$ otherwise ($i = 1, \dots, n$; $j = 1, \dots, m$).
Decision variables: $x_j = 1$ if subset $S_j$ is chosen, $x_j = 0$ otherwise.
$$\min \sum_{j=1}^{m} c_j x_j$$
$$\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_{j=1}^{m} a_{ij} x_j \ge 1, \quad i = 1, \dots, n$$
$$x_j \in \{0, 1\}, \quad j = 1, \dots, m$$
Meaning: the objective is the total cost of the chosen subsets (minimise it). The constraint for item $i$ says that at least one chosen subset contains item $i$, i.e. every item of $S$ is covered at least once. $x_j \in \{0, 1\}$: each subset is either taken or not (no fractions of a subset).

rubric.point: Defines $x_j$ (1 if $S_j$ chosen, else 0) and $a_{ij}$ (1 if item $i \in S_j$)
Constraints $\sum_j a_{ij} x_j \ge 1$ for every item $i$, $x_j \in \{0,1\}$
Meaning: every item is covered by at least one chosen subset

questions.question: A constraint of the mathematical model of the facility location problem is given by $\sum_{i=1}^{m} x_{ij} = 1$, $\forall j$, where $i$ represents the warehouses and $j$ is a customer; $x_{ij}$ is the variable representing whether customer $j$ is served by the warehouse $i$. Describe the meaning of this constraint. [2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer: For each customer $j$, the sum over all $m$ warehouses of $x_{ij}$ is exactly 1, and each $x_{ij}$ is 0 or 1. So every customer $j$ is served by exactly one warehouse: it must be served (the sum is not 0) and it cannot be split between or served by two warehouses (the sum is not 2 or more). This is the single-source requirement of the facility location model. (Another constraint, $x_{ij} \le y_i$, then makes sure that warehouse is actually open.)

rubric.point: Every customer must be served (assigned to some warehouse)
…by exactly one warehouse (single source, no splitting)

questions.explanation: Follows the handwritten solution in Past Paper Solutions 2024 Exam.pdf p. 12 ("every customer must be supplied/served by exactly 1 of the warehouses"). Course notes: DisCopt.pdf PDF p. 30 (eqs. 51–57; constraint 52 is the single-source constraint).
questions.keyDispute: The handwritten solution swaps the letters ("every customer i … of the warehouses j"); in the question $j$ is the customer and $i$ the warehouse.

questions.concept: Graph bisection: ±1 model and the 1/4 factor
questions.question:
Consider the graph bisection problem
$$\left\{\begin{array}{ll} \max_x & \frac{1}{4}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} w_{ij}(1 - x_i x_j) \\ s.t. & \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i = 0, \\ & x_i \in \{1, -1\}, i \in \{1, \cdots, n\}. \end{array}\right.$$
Let $S$ be the set of all feasible solutions to the above problem where $x_i \in \{-1, 1\}$. (i) Prove that if $x = (x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n)^T \in S$ then the solution $\bar{x} = (-x_1, -x_2, \cdots, -x_n)^T \in S$. Give your reasons as to why the objective function is multiplied by $\frac{1}{4}$. (ii) Is it possible to replace $\frac{1}{4}$ with $\frac{1}{2}$? (iii) How? [4 + 1 + 2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
(i) Let $x \in S$, so $\sum_i x_i = 0$ and every $x_i \in \{1, -1\}$. For $\bar{x} = -x$: each $\bar{x}_i = -x_i \in \{-1, 1\}$, and
$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} \bar{x}_i = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (-x_i) = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i = -0 = 0,$$
so $\bar{x} \in S$. (It is the same bisection with the two halves' labels swapped, and $\bar{x}_i\bar{x}_j = x_ix_j$, so it has the same objective value.)
Why $\frac14$: $x_i = 1$ puts $i$ in $V_1$ and $x_i = -1$ puts it in $V_2$. For a pair in the same half $x_ix_j = 1$, so $1 - x_ix_j = 0$; for a pair in different halves $x_ix_j = -1$, so $1 - x_ix_j = 2$. The double sum runs over ordered pairs, so each cut edge $\{i, j\}$ appears twice, as $(i,j)$ and $(j,i)$, with $w_{ij} = w_{ji}$:
$$w_{ij}(1 - x_ix_j) + w_{ji}(1 - x_jx_i) = 2w_{ij} + 2w_{ij} = 4w_{ij}.$$
Multiplying by $\frac14$ makes the objective exactly the total weight of the edges between $V_1$ and $V_2$ (the cut value).
(ii) Yes.
(iii) Count each pair once instead of twice, i.e. sum only over $i < j$:
$$\frac{1}{4}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} w_{ij}(1 - x_ix_j) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\sum_{j=i+1}^{n} w_{ij}(1 - x_ix_j),$$
because the diagonal terms vanish ($1 - x_i^2 = 0$) and the $(i,j)$ and $(j,i)$ terms are equal. Each cut edge now contributes $2w_{ij}$, and $\frac12$ gives $w_{ij}$. (Simply writing $\frac12$ in front of the full double sum would give twice the cut weight: the same maximiser, but not the cut value.)

rubric.point: (i) $1 - x_ix_j$ is 0 for a pair on the same side and 2 for a pair on opposite sides
(i) Each edge counted twice ($w_{ij} = w_{ji}$) gives $4w_{ij}$, so $\frac14$ makes the objective the cut weight
(iii) Sum over $i < j$ only (each pair once): $\frac12 \sum_{i<j} w_{ij}(1 - x_ix_j)$

questions.explanation: Follows the handwritten solution in Past Paper Solutions 2024 Exam.pdf p. 12 ("$w_{ij}(1 - x_ix_j) + w_{ji}(1 - x_jx_i) = 2(1 - x_ix_j)w_{ij} = 4w_{ij}$"; "yes, $\frac14 \sum\sum = \frac12 \sum_i \sum_{j>i}$"). Course notes: max-bisection model and the symmetric solution $\bar{x}$, DisCopt.pdf PDF pp. 40–41; the max-cut model with $\frac12 \sum_{i<j}$, PDF p. 42 (eq. 98). Both forms were checked numerically against the cut weight on random graphs.

questions.question: Write down the sub-tour elimination constraint for the asymmetric travelling salesman problem (ATSP). Give an example of a sub-tour that can occur for the 7-city asymmetric TSP? How does the sub-tour elimination constraint of ATSP differ from the same constraint of the symmetric travelling salesman problem (STSP)? [2+2+2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
ATSP subtour elimination constraints ($x_{ij} = 1$ if the salesman goes directly from city $i$ to city $j$):
$$\sum_{i \in S} \sum_{j \in S,\ j \ne i} x_{ij} \le |S| - 1, \qquad \forall S \subset V,\ 2 \le |S| \le n - 2.$$
For any proper subset $S$ of cities, the arcs used inside $S$ must be fewer than $|S|$, so they cannot close a cycle on $S$ alone.
Example sub-tour for 7 cities (directed): $1 \to 2 \to 1$ and $3 \to 4 \to 5 \to 6 \to 7 \to 3$. Every city has exactly one arc in and one arc out, so the assignment constraints $\sum_i x_{ij} = 1$ and $\sum_j x_{ij} = 1$ hold, but the route is two separate cycles, not one tour. It violates the subtour constraint for $S = \{1, 2\}$: $x_{12} + x_{21} = 2 > |S| - 1 = 1$.
STSP subtour elimination constraints ($x_e = 1$ if undirected edge $e$ is in the tour, $E(S)$ = edges with both ends in $S$):
$$\sum_{e \in E(S)} x_e \le |S| - 1, \qquad \forall S \subset V,\ 3 \le |S| \le n - 3.$$
Why the ranges differ: in the ATSP the arcs $(i,j)$ and $(j,i)$ are different, so two cities can form a sub-tour $i \to j \to i$; sets with $|S| = 2$ must be included. In the STSP $\{i, j\}$ is a single edge that can be used at most once, so a sub-tour needs at least 3 cities and $|S| = 2$ is not needed. The upper limit comes from the complement: if $S$ holds a sub-tour then so does $V \setminus S$, which needs at least 2 cities (ATSP, so $|S| \le n - 2$) or at least 3 cities (STSP, so $|S| \le n - 3$). The ATSP version also sums over ordered pairs $i \ne j$ instead of undirected edges.

rubric.point: ATSP constraint $\sum_{i \in S}\sum_{j \in S, j \ne i} x_{ij} \le |S| - 1$
Difference: STSP uses undirected edges $E(S)$ with $3 \le |S| \le n-3$
Reason: a 2-city sub-tour is possible only with directed arcs
